summary: Order the nodes of a directed acyclic graph so every edge points from an earlier node to a later one, typically via Kahn's BFS algorithm that repeatedly removes zero-in-degree nodes.
lesson: Topological sort answers "in what order can these tasks happen, given that some must come before others?" It only works on a directed acyclic graph, because a cycle would mean two tasks depend on each other, which has no valid order. Kahn's algorithm builds the order by repeatedly picking off any node with zero remaining prerequisites (in-degree zero), removing its outgoing edges, and repeating -- nodes that become prerequisite-free as a result get added to the queue next. If you run out of nodes to process before every node is ordered, that's proof a cycle exists somewhere in the remaining graph.
recognize_when: The problem involves prerequisites, dependencies, or 'must happen before' relationships
You're given a directed graph and asked for a valid build/execution/course order
You need to detect whether a cycle exists in a directed graph (a cycle means no valid ordering exists)
The input describes edges between tasks/courses/modules rather than an adjacency-free list
You need all valid orderings or just any one valid ordering of dependent items

complexity.notes: Each vertex is enqueued/dequeued once and each edge is examined once when decrementing in-degrees; space holds the adjacency list and in-degree/queue structures.

gotchas: Forgetting the cycle check: if len(order) != num_nodes, the graph has a cycle and no valid ordering exists
Mixing up edge direction (src -> dst means src must come before dst, not the reverse)
Not initializing in-degree for nodes with no incoming edges (they should start in the queue)
